questions.question: Q1. The Wall preset spreads satellites in azimuth but places them all at high elevation. It produces a low HDOP and a large VDOP. Why does the module treat this as a failure?

answers.a: Because HDOP below 2 is never acceptable
answers.b: Because a low horizontal DOP conceals poor vertical geometry, and an aircraft flying on that fix has an unreliable altitude despite a confident-looking horizontal position
answers.c: Because fewer than four satellites are visible
answers.d: Because high-elevation satellites have weaker signals

explanations.a: Incorrect — HDOP below 2 is the pass condition for the horizontal component.
explanations.b: Correct — this is the trap the preset exists to spring. Reporting only a 2-D DOP hides a vertical solution that is badly conditioned, which matters enormously to an aircraft.
explanations.c: Incorrect — the preset uses the full satellite count you have selected.
explanations.d: Incorrect — high-elevation satellites generally have the best signal path; geometry, not signal strength, is the problem.

questions.question: Q2. Keeping the constellation fixed and switching ranging from Open-sky (UERE 3.0 m) to Urban (UERE 7.5 m) causes the fix cloud to expand by a factor of 2.5. What does that show about DOP?

answers.b: DOP is a pure geometry multiplier; the metres of error come from multiplying it by the ranging error, so identical geometry gives very different accuracy in different environments
answers.c: Urban environments reduce the number of satellites

explanations.a: Incorrect — DOP is unchanged here, which is precisely the point of holding the constellation fixed.
explanations.b: Correct — CEP = HDOP x UERE. Good geometry cannot rescue poor ranging, and the same constellation is worth 2.5 times less in a multipath environment.
explanations.c: Incorrect — the satellite count is unchanged in this comparison.
explanations.d: Incorrect — CEP is directly proportional to UERE.

questions.question: Q3. Module 1 passes only when HDOP is below 2 AND CEP is below 4 m. Why are two conditions required rather than one?

answers.a: They are redundant; either alone would do
answers.b: They test different things: HDOP checks that the geometry is well conditioned, CEP checks that the resulting position error in metres is actually small enough to fly on
answers.c: CEP is a backup in case HDOP cannot be computed
answers.d: The second condition only applies below four satellites

explanations.a: Incorrect — good geometry with poor ranging passes the first and fails the second, as the urban case demonstrates.
explanations.b: Correct — a dimensionless conditioning number and a physical distance are separate criteria. Requiring both prevents a well-conditioned but inaccurate solution from being accepted.
explanations.c: Incorrect — both are computed whenever a solution exists.
explanations.d: Incorrect — below four satellites there is no solution at all.

questions.question: Q4. A GPS fix requires at least four satellites. Given that position is three coordinates, why is the fourth needed?

answers.a: For redundancy in case one signal is lost
answers.b: To solve for receiver clock bias, which is a fourth unknown because the receiver has no atomic clock of its own
answers.d: To determine which satellites are healthy

explanations.a: Incorrect — redundancy is a benefit of extra satellites beyond four, not the reason for the fourth.
explanations.b: Correct — the receiver measures pseudoranges contaminated by an unknown clock offset. With four unknowns you need at least four independent measurements.
explanations.c: Incorrect — signal quality is a separate matter from the number of unknowns.
explanations.d: Incorrect — satellite health is broadcast in the navigation message.

questions.question: Q5. Individual fixes are drawn from a Rayleigh radial distribution whose median radius equals the current CEP. What does CEP therefore mean?

answers.a: The maximum possible error, which is never exceeded
answers.b: The radius within which half of all fixes fall, so half of them land outside it
answers.c: The average of all radial errors
answers.d: The error at exactly one standard deviation

explanations.a: Incorrect — this is a common and dangerous misreading. CEP bounds nothing.
explanations.b: Correct — Circular Error Probable is the 50% radius. Half your fixes are worse than the quoted figure, which is why an obstacle clearance sized to CEP is inadequate.
explanations.c: Incorrect — for a Rayleigh distribution the mean radius is slightly larger than the median.
explanations.d: Incorrect — one sigma corresponds to roughly 68% for a normal variable, a different quantity.

questions.question: Q6. The barometric sweep runs 0 to 3000 m automatically and ignores the True Altitude slider. Why does the module sweep instead of testing a single altitude?

answers.a: To make the run take longer
answers.b: Because the diagnostic information is in how the error grows with height, which distinguishes random sensor noise from a systematic modelling bias
answers.c: Because the sensor cannot be read at a fixed altitude
answers.d: Because the slider is broken in this module

explanations.a: Incorrect — the sweep exists to produce a curve, not to consume time.
explanations.b: Correct — a coarse sensor scatters roughly uniformly with height, while a temperature inversion produces a bias proportional to height. Only the shape of the curve separates them, and a single point cannot.
explanations.c: Incorrect — it can, and the telemetry does so continuously outside a run.
explanations.d: Incorrect — the slider is used by Module 3; this module deliberately overrides it.

questions.question: Q7. A temperature inversion is described as a systematic bias rather than added noise. Why does that distinction matter to a flight controller?

answers.a: It does not; both raise the reported error equally
answers.b: Noise averages out over time while a bias does not, so filtering removes the first and leaves the second intact in the altitude estimate
answers.d: Noise is always the more dangerous of the two

explanations.a: Incorrect — they behave completely differently under filtering, which is the practical difference.
explanations.b: Correct — a low-pass filter or a longer averaging window reduces zero-mean noise but is powerless against a consistent offset. The aircraft holds a confident, smooth, wrong altitude.
explanations.c: Incorrect — the inversion bias is a barometric altitude error, so it is vertical.
explanations.d: Incorrect — noise is generally the more tractable of the two, precisely because it can be filtered.

questions.question: Q8. Module 3 combines horizontal and vertical errors as Total = sqrt(CEP^2 + h_err^2) rather than adding them. What does that assume, and what is the consequence?

answers.a: It assumes the errors are identical and simply averages them
answers.b: It assumes the two error sources are statistically independent, so they combine in quadrature; the larger term therefore dominates and reducing the smaller one buys very little
answers.c: It assumes the vertical error is always negligible
answers.d: It assumes both errors are worst-case and adds a safety factor

explanations.a: Incorrect — quadrature combination is not an average.
explanations.b: Correct — GNSS geometry and barometric pressure sensing are unrelated mechanisms, so a root-sum-square is appropriate. The practical consequence is that engineering effort belongs on whichever term is larger.
explanations.c: Incorrect — the vertical term is explicitly included and can dominate.
explanations.d: Incorrect — RSS is a statistical combination, not a conservative worst case; simple addition would be more conservative.

questions.question: Q9. A build reports CEP of 3.0 m and barometric error of 1.3 m, giving a 3-D radius of about 3.3 m against a 5 m safety threshold. Which improvement would help most, and why?

answers.a: Improving the barometer, because 1.3 m is the easier number to reduce
answers.b: Improving the horizontal fix, because in quadrature the 3.0 m term contributes about 9.0 of the 10.7 total, so the vertical term is nearly irrelevant
answers.c: Both contribute equally, so either is fine
answers.d: Neither, since the build already passes

explanations.a: Incorrect — even eliminating the barometric error entirely would only move the total from 3.3 m to 3.0 m.
explanations.b: Correct — squaring exaggerates the dominant term. Effort spent on the smaller contributor is almost entirely wasted, which is the main practical use of an error budget.
explanations.c: Incorrect — they contribute in a roughly 9 to 1.7 ratio once squared.
explanations.d: Incorrect — it passes, but understanding which term dominates is what lets you keep it passing as conditions worsen.

questions.question: Q10. Modules 2 and 3 stay locked until the constellation check passes. What is the engineering justification for that ordering?

answers.a: It is purely a user-interface convention with no technical basis
answers.b: The horizontal fix is an input to the combined error budget, so characterising the altimeter or synthesising a total radius is meaningless until the horizontal solution is known to be valid
answers.c: The barometer cannot physically operate without GPS lock
answers.d: The modules share a sensor that can only be used by one at a time

explanations.a: Incorrect — the dependency is real, not cosmetic.
explanations.b: Correct — Module 3 consumes the CEP from Module 1 and the altitude error from Module 2. Building a budget on an invalid or singular horizontal solution would produce a number with no meaning.
explanations.c: Incorrect — a barometer is entirely independent of GNSS and works with no satellites at all.
explanations.d: Incorrect — the sensors are separate and operate simultaneously.
